q: Pear, spice and a broad soft texture, often with a trace of sugar left in, describe a white that went from almost nothing to one of the country's most planted. Which variety?
opts: Chenin Blanc
Pinot Gris
Viognier
Semillon
exp: Pinot Gris arrived late and spread quickly, offering drinkers a rounder alternative to the Sauvignon Blanc that surrounds them. Styles run from bone dry in the Alsace manner to noticeably sweet, so the producer rather than the variety decides what turns up in the glass.

q: From tightly wound barrel-fermented bottlings in the north to Gisborne's broad tropical ones, this grape is taken seriously in almost every New Zealand region. Which?
opts: Riesling
Sauvignon Blanc
Chardonnay
Pinot Gris
exp: Chardonnay takes its character from the site and the cellar rather than from itself, which is why it turns up everywhere and tastes different each time. New Zealand's examples are built on high natural acidity, so they carry oak and lees work without turning heavy.

q: Outside the warmest gravels of Hawke's Bay and Waiheke, Cabernet Sauvignon struggles to finish ripening in New Zealand. Which Bordeaux grape carries most of the country's red blends instead?
opts: Carmenere
Merlot
Petit Verdot
Malbec
exp: Merlot ripens earlier and far more dependably in a maritime autumn, and it gives flesh where Cabernet gives structure. Cabernet Franc and Malbec appear in the same blends in smaller proportions, and Petit Verdot ripens even later than Cabernet Sauvignon, so it is planted barely at all.

q: A three-year-old New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc still smells of passionfruit and cut grass. Which property of the closure it wears is doing that work?
opts: It admits more oxygen than cork, which keeps the wine lively
It allows a slow secondary fermentation to carry on in bottle
It slowly releases sulphur dioxide into the bottle headspace
It admits very little oxygen, and at the same rate in every bottle
exp: Thiols and pyrazines are fragile and oxidise readily, so an aromatic white loses its entire point if the seal leaks. Consistency matters as much as the low ingress: a case sealed with cork varies bottle to bottle, and a case under screwcap does not.

q: An expensive New Zealand red built to spend twenty years in a cellar is very likely to be sealed the same way as a supermarket Sauvignon Blanc. What does that reveal about the country's approach to closures?
opts: Cork is reserved by law for wines above a set price
Screwcaps are permitted on white wine only
The screwcap is used right across the range rather than treated as a budget option
Screwcaps were adopted because cork cannot be obtained in the southern hemisphere
exp: New Zealand producers moved together at the start of the 2000s rather than one winery at a time, and the change reached the top of the range as fast as the bottom. The argument since has not been whether to use a screwcap but how much oxygen the liner should let through for a wine meant to age.

q: An independently audited national scheme scores New Zealand growers on soil, water, agrichemicals, energy, waste and the people they employ, and almost the whole producing vineyard area takes part. What is it called?
opts: Integrated Production of Wine
Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand
Entwine
The Wine Standards Board
exp: The programme began in the mid-1990s and grew into a condition of joining the industry's own export marketing, which is why participation is close to universal rather than a minority badge. Entwine was the Australian scheme until it was folded into Sustainable Winegrowing Australia in 2019, and Integrated Production of Wine is the South African one.

q: A bottle certified organic in New Zealand has met a different standard from the national sustainability programme most of the country's vineyards belong to. Where do the two part company?
opts: The organic standard applies to exports and the sustainability scheme to the home market
They are the same scheme operating under two different names
Organic certification governs the winery only, and the sustainability scheme the vineyard only
Organic certification bans synthetic agrichemicals outright, while the sustainability scheme only limits them
exp: A sustainability audit measures and limits agrichemical use inside a wider scorecard that takes in energy, water, waste and employment, so it covers ground the organic standard never touches. What it does not do is prohibit a synthetic spray outright, and that single difference is why a producer might pursue both certifications at once.

q: Rainfall falls and heat rises steadily as you travel from the Minho down to the Alentejo. Which climatic shift does that describe?
opts: Mediterranean conditions in the north giving way to maritime conditions in the south
One uniform Mediterranean climate across the whole mainland
Alpine conditions in the north giving way to desert in the south
Atlantic maritime in the north-west giving way to Mediterranean conditions in the south
exp: The north-west takes the weather off the ocean full in the face and can receive well over a metre of rain a year, while the southern plains bake through a long dry summer. Almost every difference in Portuguese wine style follows that line.

q: A Portuguese label carries no DOC and no village, yet still claims a broad origin such as Alentejano or Lisboa. Which tier is that?
opts: Denominacao de Origem Controlada
Vinho Regional
Indicacao de Proveniencia Regulamentada
Vinho
exp: Vinho Regional is Portugal's equivalent of a French IGP: wider boundaries, a longer list of permitted grapes and the freedom to name a variety on the label. Plain Vinho makes no geographical claim at all.

q: Some Portuguese demarcated areas spent years in a probationary rank abbreviated IPR before promotion. Where did that rank sit?
opts: Above DOC, as a superior classification for the finest estates
Alongside DOC, covering fortified wine only
Between Vinho Regional and DOC, for candidate appellations
Below plain Vinho, for wine that had failed inspection
exp: Indicacao de Proveniencia Regulamentada marked an area whose rules were already fixed but whose track record was not yet long enough for DOC. Most were eventually promoted or folded into a regional name, and the tier has all but vanished under EU labelling.

q: Mountain ranges standing between the coast and the interior are decisive for Portuguese wine. What do they chiefly do?
opts: Funnel Atlantic rain inland, keeping the interior wet
Cool the coastal strip by shading it from the afternoon sun
Trap cold air on the plateau, bringing frost through the summer
Block Atlantic rain and cloud, leaving hot dry conditions inland
exp: The Marao and Montemuro shield the Douro, and the Caramulo and Serra da Estrela ring the Dao. In both cases a maritime climate becomes a hot, dry, continental one within a few dozen kilometres.

q: Guests often assume the green in Vinho Verde refers to the colour in the glass. What does the word actually indicate?
opts: That the region's wines must by law be sold in green glass
That the wine is made to be drunk young, soon after the harvest
That the fruit is picked unripe and the wine is high in malic acid
That the wine takes a green tinge from long storage in stainless steel
exp: Verde here means youthful rather than coloured, and the wines were traditionally sold within months of the vintage. The region also makes red and rose under the same name, which no colour reading can explain.

q: Bounded by the Minho river along the Spanish border and by the Douro to the south, which region occupies that corner of Portugal?
opts: Dao
Bairrada
Vinho Verde
Tras-os-Montes
exp: The Minho province is the wettest and greenest corner of the country, granite underfoot and Atlantic weather overhead. That rainfall drives both the training systems and the light, sharp style.

q: Traditional Minho smallholdings trained vines high overhead on pergolas and even up living trees. Which two problems did that solve at once?
opts: Other crops could grow underneath and the canopy stayed clear of damp ground
Sugar levels rose sharply and the wine finished higher in alcohol
Yields fell sharply, and the smaller crop that remained ripened to a higher sugar
Spring frost was avoided and summer irrigation became unnecessary
exp: Holdings were tiny and had to feed a family, so cabbages and maize grew beneath the fruit. Lifting the canopy also kept it out of the still, humid air at ground level, where rot thrives in a region this wet.

q: A young Vinho Verde arrives at the table with a faint prickle of gas. Where did that traditionally come from?
opts: Carbon dioxide left over from a fortification step
A second alcoholic fermentation deliberately induced in bottle
Extended lees contact in tank through the winter
Malolactic conversion finishing after the wine was already in bottle
exp: The old wines went into bottle unstable and finished their malolactic there, which threw a light spritz and often a haze. Modern producers ferment out, filter, and inject a measured dose of carbon dioxide at bottling instead.

q: Along the Minho river in the far north lies a warmer, drier pocket that is the traditional home of Alvarinho. Which sub-region?
opts: Moncao e Melgaco
Paiva
Basto
Lima
exp: Moncao e Melgaco sits in a rain shadow behind the Serra da Peneda, which lets Alvarinho reach a ripeness it cannot find elsewhere in the region. The same grape is Albarino across the river in Rias Baixas.
